design_detail: Mixed-methods study in two parts, both online (Qualtrics), approved by the University College London Research Ethics Committee and explicitly not pre-registered. Study 1 (qualitative, described here and not rated): written answers to four open questions from 16 attendees of psilocybin retreats at four collaborating centres in the Netherlands and Mexico, selected for reporting both distress during ceremonies and significant personal transformation; inductive thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke) with two researchers coding independently in NVivo. Its themes, with the literature, were used to write a new 26-item inventory of responses to challenging experiences (ReCiPE). Study 2 (quantitative, rated with ROBINS-E): a self-selected online survey advertised through social media, research groups and forums to people who had used a classic psychedelic; of 869 completers, 555 reported a period of distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported experience and 529 were analysed. Each strategy was rated not tried, tried and not helpful, somewhat helpful or substantially helpful, then scored 1 if tried and judged helpful; exploratory factor analysis (WLSMV on tetrachoric correlations, Geomin rotation); Pearson correlations of ReCiPE factor counts and CEQ subscales with the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI); and a multiple regression of EBI on the CEQ and ReCiPE factors that correlated with it. All ratings are retrospective self-report by the same person, in some cases years after the experience.
can_establish: What kinds of responses 16 retreat attendees who reported both difficulty and transformation described using during challenging psilocybin ceremonies; and, among 529 self-selected people recalling a challenging psychedelic experience, how many said they tried each of 26 strategies and found it helpful, how those judgments grouped, and how the number of strategies judged helpful and the kind of challenge went with retrospectively rated emotional breakthrough.
cannot_establish: Whether any strategy shortens, eases or resolves a challenging experience or brings about emotional breakthrough (helpfulness is the respondent's own retrospective judgment, scored only when the strategy was judged helpful, and correlated with an outcome rated by the same person at the same time; no comparison, manipulation or prospective measurement); how often these strategies are used or helpful among people who use psychedelics in general; or whether the findings hold in clinical, ceremonial or recreational settings specifically (setting, substance and amount are not analysed).

sample.recruitment: Study 1: attendees of psilocybin retreats at four collaborating centres in the Netherlands (8) and Mexico (8), contacted by email if they had agreed to research contact (Methods › Study 1 › Participants and recruitment). Study 2: online survey advertised to people with psychedelic experience through targeted social media, research groups and forums (Methods › Study 2 › Participants and recruitment). n_total counts the 16 plus the 529 analysed.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both studies: aged 18 or over, proficient in English, prior psychedelic experience, electronic consent. Study 1 additionally: prior psilocybin retreat attendance and self-reported significant personal transformation together with distress or difficulty during ceremonies. Study 2: at least one experience with psilocybin, ayahuasca, LSD, DMT or mescaline; experiences limited to MDMA, ketamine or other non-classic psychedelics excluded, combined use allowed; only those reporting distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported experience completed the CEQ and ReCiPE.
sample.demographics: Study 1: mean age 45; 9 women, 7 men; 13 with no religious affiliation; 15 with graduate or postgraduate education; retreats of 3 to 7 days with up to 3 ceremonies; median 6 months since attendance. Study 2 (n = 529): 243 men (45.94%), 256 women (48.39%), 30 non-binary or other (5.67%); mean age 37.71 (SD 10.88). Substance, setting, time since the experience and lifetime psychedelic experience were collected but are reported only in Supplementary Material S.VI (a docx file, not read).
sample.attrition: Study 2: 26 of the 555 who reported a challenge (4.7%) were not analysed, without a stated reason; the regression's degrees of freedom imply 527 cases. The number who started the survey but did not complete it is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Both samples self-selected. Study 1 was chosen for reporting transformation, so its accounts describe challenges that ended well, as the authors note. Study 2 was recruited where people interested in psychedelics gather and, by the authors' account, consisted mainly of experienced people from Western cultures who may have developed effective coping over time (Discussion, 9th paragraph). The main text does not say how respondents chose which experience to report.

exposure.measurement: ReCiPE, a new 26-item inventory written from the Study 1 themes and the literature: for each strategy, not tried, tried and not helpful, tried and somewhat helpful, tried and substantially helpful. For factor analysis, correlations and regression the answers were turned into a binary score (1 = tried and judged somewhat or substantially helpful), so a factor 'score' is the number of strategies judged helpful, not how often or how much a strategy was used (Methods › Study 2 › Measures › Responses to challenging psychedelic experiences). Kinds of challenge were measured with the CEQ subscales. The scale is in the supplement (cited as S.II in the Methods and S.V in the Results).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not analysed. Substance and time since the experience were collected (reported in supplement S.VI only); amount, route and setting of the reported experience are not reported in the article. Study 1 concerned psilocybin retreat ceremonies, with amounts not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Combined use with non-classic psychedelics was allowed in Study 2 but not recorded in the article. One ReCiPE item asks about taking another drug or drinking alcohol during the challenge: 12.1% of the 529 tried it and judged it helpful; it did not load on any factor.

comparison.controls: None. Associations are within the 529 people who reported a challenge; no group without the strategies or without a challenge was compared on the same measures.
comparison.matching: None; the regression contains no covariates other than the CEQ and ReCiPE factors.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Personality and habitual emotion regulation (which the authors name as possible explanations), psychiatric history, prior psychedelic experience, setting (therapeutic, ceremonial or recreational), substance and amount, presence and behaviour of others, and time since the experience: not used in any analysis.

outcomes.instruments: Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (EBI; Roseman et al., 2019): 6 items on a 0 to 100 visual analogue scale, averaged; single factor explaining 71.4% of variance, Cronbach's alpha .918 in this sample. Challenging Experience Questionnaire (CEQ; Barrett et al., 2016): 26 items, 0 to 5, seven subscales (fear, grief, physical distress, insanity, isolation, death, paranoia), alpha at least .928; an added trauma-reliving item was not analysed. ReCiPE alphas: total .801; Acceptance and Reappraisal .726 without its weakly loading item (.718 with it, as kept), Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction .731 without its two weakly loading items (.716 with them, as kept), Social Support and Disclosure .786.
outcomes.validity_norms: The EBI and CEQ are published validated scales; the ReCiPE is new, its three-factor structure is preliminary and chosen partly on interpretability, the fit indices are described only as passing thresholds without values, and the authors say it needs further validation with an interval scoring scheme (Discussion, 10th paragraph). The EBI was chosen as outcome because it suits a mixed non-clinical group.
outcomes.operationalization: 'Emotional breakthrough' is the mean EBI score for the reported experience, rated by the respondent at the time of the survey. 'Helpful strategy' is the respondent's own judgment of helpfulness, made at the same time, about a strategy used during the same experience.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None; alpha .05 throughout. 62 counts the 55 correlations in Table 3 and the 7 regression coefficients in Table 4.

analysis.effect_sizes: Correlations with EBI (Table 3, n = 529): Acceptance and Reappraisal r = 0.50, Social Support and Disclosure 0.27, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction 0.18; CEQ grief 0.41, death 0.20, physical distress 0.10, fear -0.14; insanity -0.07, isolation -0.03, paranoia -0.08 (not significant). Fear correlated with fewer acceptance (r = -0.20) and sensory (-0.14) strategies judged helpful; grief with more acceptance (0.19) and social-support (0.24) strategies. Regression (Table 4): F(7, 519) = 50.93, adjusted R-squared 0.399 (R-squared change 0.407); standardized beta: grief 0.37, acceptance and reappraisal 0.33, death 0.17, social support and disclosure 0.07 (p = .041), fear -0.24 (all others p < .001); physical distress -0.02 (p = .693) and sensory regulation 0.02 (p = .527) not significant. Editors' calculation from t multiplied by SE in Table 4: unstandardized coefficients of about 7.0 EBI points per unit of CEQ grief, -4.5 per unit of fear, 2.6 per unit of death, 4.1 per acceptance strategy judged helpful and 1.2 per social-support strategy. No covariates.
analysis.covariates: None. The regression predictors were the variables that correlated significantly with the EBI.
analysis.preregistration_detail: The Methods state that neither study was pre-registered (Methods, 1st paragraph).
analysis.selective_reporting: Predictors entered the regression only if they correlated significantly with the outcome, which inflates the variance explained and the coefficients. The fit indices of the factor solutions, the per-item frequencies (Figure 1, an image, and supplement S.VII), and the substance, setting and timing of the reported experiences (supplement S.VI) are not in the text. The text says unstandardized coefficients and their intervals were reported, but Table 4 has no unstandardized column.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Retreat attendees described four families of responses to difficult ceremonies (inner responses, embodied practice and engagement with the environment, interpersonal responses, and responses from facilitators). In 529 self-selected people recalling a challenging experience, letting go or surrendering (84.5%), observing the mind without fighting it (77.3%) and closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (73.9%) were the strategies most often tried and judged helpful; anger or aggression (9.4%), trying to sleep (9.7%), telling the experience to stop (10.6%) and taking another drug or alcohol (12.1%) the least. Respondents who judged more acceptance-and-reappraisal and social-support strategies helpful, and who reported more grief- and death-type and less fear-type challenge, rated their emotional breakthrough higher, all measured at one retrospective sitting.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract stays mostly with associational wording but says the findings offer insights for "enhancing safety in both clinical and non-clinical settings", and no safety outcome was measured. The discussion opens by saying the research examined the effectiveness of strategies (Discussion, 1st paragraph), whereas it measured self-judged helpfulness; it says the correlations confirm that breakthrough involves adopting more helpful strategies (Discussion, 3rd paragraph), a causal reading of cross-sectional data in which helpfulness may itself reflect how the experience ended; and it proposes that ACT-based preparation could reduce a direct effect of fear on breakthrough and raise an indirect effect through acceptance (Discussion, 8th paragraph), mediation language without any mediation analysis. The text also interprets the standardized coefficients as unstandardized slopes (a rise of 0.37 in breakthrough per unit of grief), which understates the implied unstandardized slope of about 7 points (Results › Multiple regression, 3rd paragraph). The limitations paragraphs are frank about self-selection, retrospective recall and the new scale, and the discussion notes that set and setting could explain the associations.

timeline.event: Carbonaro et al. survey of challenging experiences with psilocybin mushrooms and Barrett et al.'s Challenging Experience Questionnaire, both used here as background and measure (as cited).
Roseman et al. validate the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory used as this study's outcome (as cited).

Simonsson et al. quota-stratified US survey, cited here: 'trying to calm the mind' was the action most often reported as helpful during the most challenging experience (41.9% of 613), a pattern in line with the acceptance strategies most often judged helpful here
This study: first version of the ReCiPE, with a preliminary three-factor structure and cross-sectional associations with emotional breakthrough.

replication.where_it_stands: A first, exploratory instrument-development study. No independent sample has tested the ReCiPE's structure, and no study has measured strategies during or immediately after sessions, or manipulated them (for example through preparation that teaches acceptance), to test whether they change how a challenging experience unfolds.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article. The competing-interests declaration notes that R.G.M is supported by the Wellcome Trust.
funding.declared_conflicts: As printed: the authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Research Department of Clinical, Educational and Health Psychology and the Clinical Psychopharmacology Unit, University College London. Study 1 participants came through four collaborating retreat centres, with which one author liaised (author contributions); the centres and any arrangement with them are not named. The discussion's recommendations on preparation cite the second author's own scale of psychedelic preparedness and digital preparation intervention (refs 30 and 88). Recorded as flags for closer reading, not as reasons to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A randomized comparison of preparation that teaches acceptance and reappraisal skills against an attention-matched control, in people about to take part in a psilocybin session in a clinical or retreat setting, with challenge (CEQ) and breakthrough (EBI) rated within a day and strategy use recorded during or right after the session by participants and by blinded observers; together with an independent confirmatory factor analysis of the ReCiPE.

domains.note: Study 2 regression has no covariates: setting, substance, amount, prior experience, personality and habitual emotion regulation could all drive both the strategies judged helpful and emotional breakthrough, as the authors acknowledge for set and setting.

New, preliminarily validated inventory; the score counts only strategies judged helpful, a retrospective judgment that is likely shaped by how the experience ended, which is close to the outcome itself.
Self-selected through psychedelic forums, research groups and social media; only people reporting a challenge were analysed; the way the reported experience was chosen is not described.

What others did during the experience (facilitators, friends, therapists) and any later integration work could affect both strategy judgments and breakthrough ratings; not recorded except as ReCiPE items.
26 of 555 respondents with a challenge were not analysed and the regression has 527 cases, without explanation or a stated method for missing data.
EBI rated retrospectively, sometimes years later, by the same person who judged the strategies, with knowledge of both.

Not pre-registered; regression predictors chosen because they correlated significantly with the outcome; factor solution chosen partly on interpretability; printed intervals inconsistent with the estimates.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised as a cross-sectional exposure-outcome study (ROBINS-E) for Study 2; Study 1 is described, not rated. Study 1 is a reasonable catalogue of responses, with two independent coders and attributed quotations, but it rests on 16 highly educated retreat attendees chosen for transformative outcomes, written answers without follow-up questions, and no reflexivity or saturation account; it says nothing about frequency or effect. In Study 2, the associations between strategies judged helpful and emotional breakthrough are at very high risk of bias: no confounders were adjusted for, both measures are retrospective ratings by the same person, the strategy score depends on a helpfulness judgment that partly reflects the outcome, and the regression was built from significant correlations. Cite the paper for the strategies people described and for the share of this self-selected sample who said they tried each strategy and found it helpful, labelled as self-judged; not for any strategy being effective, and not for the regression coefficients as effect sizes.

key_findings.finding: Study 1: 16 psilocybin retreat attendees (8 Netherlands, 8 Mexico; retreats of 3 to 7 days with up to 3 ceremonies; median 6 months since attendance; mean age 45; 9 women; 15 with graduate or postgraduate education) wrote about challenging episodes.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 1: qualitative analysis › Participant characteristics

key_findings.finding: Study 1 themes of responses to difficult ceremonies: inner responses (accepting and observing; self-talk and reassurance; interrogating or commanding the challenge; interpretation and meaning-making; journaling); embodied practice and engagement with the environment (intentional breathing; opening the eyes and moving around rather than lying still, one participant having been encouraged to stay lying with an eye mask; sensory engagement with the surroundings and the ceremony; leaving the ceremony; sleep); interpersonal responses (avoiding others; asking for help; disclosure); and facilitator responses (touch and reminders to breathe; listening; reassurance, which one participant found unhelpful when it was evasive; rhythm and sound; introducing new elements).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 1: qualitative analysis › Thematic analysis, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Study 2: of 869 survey completers, 555 reported distress, difficulty or discomfort during their reported psychedelic experience and 529 were analysed: 243 men (45.94%), 256 women (48.39%), 30 non-binary or other (5.67%); mean age 37.71 (SD 10.88).
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: 555 of 869 is 63.87%, not the printed 64.24% (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Share of the 529 who tried a strategy and judged it somewhat or substantially helpful: letting go, accepting or surrendering 84.5%; observing the mind and not fighting it 77.3%; closing the eyes, lying or sitting down 73.9%. Least often: directing anger or aggression at the experience 9.4%, trying to fall asleep 9.7%, assertively telling it to stop or go away 10.6%, taking another drug or consuming alcohol 12.1%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 2nd paragraph; Figure 1 legend
key_findings.note: These percentages are of all 529 and combine how often a strategy was tried with how often it was judged helpful. Per-item counts for not tried and tried-but-not-helpful are only in Figure 1 (figure image not viewable; values not extracted) and supplement S.VII (not read).

key_findings.finding: Respondents judged on average 11.25 strategies helpful (SD 4.78; mode 10) of 26: Acceptance and Reappraisal 5.25 (SD 2.39) of 11, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction 3.82 (SD 2.41) of 10, Social Support and Disclosure 2.17 (SD 1.80; mode 0) of 5.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Descriptive statistics, 3rd paragraph; Reliability, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Exploratory factor analysis of the binary ReCiPE favoured three factors (two-factor solution fit poorly; three and four factors fit similarly, three chosen as more coherent with fewer cross-loadings): Acceptance and Reappraisal, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction, Social Support and Disclosure; factor correlations 0.330, 0.118 and 0.217. Telling the experience to stop, trying to sleep and taking another drug or alcohol loaded below 0.4 on every factor but were kept, so Factor 1 counts 11 strategies (letting go, observing the mind, questioning the challenge, telling it to stop, directing anger or aggression at it (0.43), interpreting sensations as meaningful, journaling, focusing on breathing, closing the eyes or lying or sitting down (cross-loading), asking forgiveness, calling on spirits or a deity), Factor 2 ten (including trying to sleep and taking another drug or alcohol) and Factor 3 five. Alphas: total .801; Factor 1 .726 without telling it to stop (.718 with it, as kept), Factor 2 .731 without its two weakly loading items (.716 with them, as kept), Factor 3 .786.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Factor analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2; Reliability, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Correlations with the Emotional Breakthrough Inventory (Table 3 prints no n; 529 were analysed and the regression used 527): Acceptance and Reappraisal r = 0.50, Social Support and Disclosure 0.27, Sensory Regulation and Physical Interaction 0.18; CEQ grief 0.41, death 0.20, physical distress 0.10, fear -0.14; insanity, isolation and paranoia not significant. Fear went with fewer acceptance strategies judged helpful (r = -0.20); grief with more acceptance (0.19) and social-support (0.24) strategies.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Correlations; Table 3

key_findings.finding: Regression of emotional breakthrough on four CEQ and three ReCiPE factors: F(7, 519) = 50.93, p < .001, adjusted R-squared 0.399; standardized beta grief 0.37, acceptance and reappraisal 0.33, fear -0.24, death 0.17 (all p < .001), social support and disclosure 0.07 (p = .041); physical distress -0.02 (p = .693) and sensory regulation and physical interaction 0.02 (p = .527) not significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study 2: online survey › Multiple regression, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 4 and its note
key_findings.note: Printed intervals and the text's reading of the coefficients are inconsistent with Table 4 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Neither study was pre-registered; the regression's predictors were the variables that correlated significantly with emotional breakthrough; no covariates were included; alpha .05 throughout.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Study 2: online survey › Data analysis, 1st paragraph and Multiple regression

key_findings.finding: The authors' limitations: both samples self-selected; mainly experienced people from Western cultures who may have developed effective coping; retrospective reports, some of experiences years earlier; Study 1 selected for transformative outcomes; varied settings and motives in Study 2; the ReCiPE is new and its binary scoring loses information; direct clinical applicability limited.

reporting_issues.issue: 555 of 869 completers is printed as 64.24%; 555/869 is 63.87% (64.24% would correspond to a denominator of about 864).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but it suggests an unreported exclusion before the 869 or a different denominator; the flow from survey starts to the analysed 529 is not fully described.

reporting_issues.issue: The regression's F(7, 519) implies 527 cases, while the analysed sample is 529; no missing-data handling is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Two cases are unaccounted for; minor for the estimates, but the sample flow cannot be reconstructed.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 4 prints standardized betas beside standard errors and t values that belong to unstandardized coefficients (for fear, -0.24 with SE 0.81 and t = -5.50, which implies B of about -4.5), and lists the intercept (29.33) in the beta column. The text then reads the standardized betas as unstandardized slopes (a rise of 0.37 in breakthrough for each unit of grief) and says unstandardized coefficients were reported, though no such column exists.
reporting_issues.consequence: The text's interpretation of slope sizes is wrong by more than an order of magnitude: the implied unstandardized slope for grief is about 7 EBI points per CEQ unit (editors' calculation from t and SE).

reporting_issues.issue: The 95% interval printed for Acceptance and Reappraisal (0.16 to 0.26) does not contain its own estimate (beta = 0.33); the intervals for death (0.07 to 0.19 around 0.17), grief (0.28 to 0.42 around 0.37) and fear (−0.30 to −0.14 around −0.24) are lopsided. None can be reproduced from Table 4 (editors' calculation gives about 0.25 to 0.41 for acceptance by rescaling the interval of B).
reporting_issues.consequence: The printed intervals cannot be used; the significance of these predictors is not in doubt (t = 8.29, 4.45 and 9.78), but their precision should be quoted from Table 4's t values, not from the text.

reporting_issues.issue: The location of the ReCiPE is given as Supplementary Material S.II in the Methods and as S.V in the Results; S.II is also cited for the qualitative findings.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; readers looking for the scale must check both sections of the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: The factor named Acceptance and Reappraisal is a count of 11 strategies judged helpful that, besides letting go, observing the mind and reappraisal items, includes two confrontational responses, assertively telling the experience to stop (item 4, loading 0.17, kept) and directing anger or aggression at it (item 5, 0.43), as well as journaling, focusing on breathing, closing the eyes or lying down (cross-loading), asking forgiveness and calling on spirits or a deity. The abstract reports the factor's association with emotional breakthrough under its label, and the Discussion links it to acceptance-based preparation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2 and its note; Results › Study 2: online survey › Factor analysis, 2nd paragraph; Reliability, 1st paragraph; Abstract; Discussion, 4th and 8th paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: The r = 0.50 and beta 0.33 belong to a mixed count, not to acceptance alone; cite them as the 11 strategies the authors grouped as acceptance and reappraisal, naming what the group includes.
